routeReviews.routeRationale: The transcript presents a coherent route from apparently gratuitous suffering and confused salvation requirements to the irrationality of classical theism, while also challenging the arguments from reason, design, and morality.

bridgeReviews.rationale: Woodford explicitly concludes that belief in the all-powerful, all-loving God under discussion is irrational given the available evidence.
Woodford argues that the problem of evil prevents the cumulative positive arguments, even if granted, from identifying the proposed all-powerful, all-loving God.
The transcript repeatedly contrasts pervasive apparently purposeless suffering with an all-powerful, all-loving God and argues that merely possible theodicies do not establish rational belief.
Woodford argues that grave postmortem consequences are incompatible with an all-loving God when sincere people and religious communities cannot reliably determine the conditions of salvation.
Woodford uses evolutionary explanations of reliable cognition, moral intuitions, disagreement, and apparent biological design to challenge the claim that those phenomena identify God.

routeReviews.routeRationale: The transcript presents a cumulative case for rational theism from reason, fine-tuning, and objective morality and separately offers responses intended to prevent suffering from defeating that case.

bridgeReviews.rationale: Edwards explicitly concludes that the cumulative evidence makes God's existence more probable and belief in God more rational than the alternative.
Edwards combines the arguments from rational minds, fine-tuning, and morality and later argues that suffering is strong counterevidence but not a defeater.
Edwards argues that unguided evolution selects primarily for survival rather than truth, whereas an intelligent creator explains trustworthy minds and an intelligible universe.
Edwards argues that the universe's narrowly life-permitting physical conditions are vastly less plausible by chance than under intelligent design.
Edwards argues that objective moral obligations are difficult to explain in an impersonal universe but intelligible when goodness is grounded in God.

moveReviews.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moveReviews.attributionBasis: The source span lies within Woodford's uninterrupted opening presentation after the moderator explicitly invites him to begin his case against rational theism.
moveReviews.rationale: The move defines rational belief as accordance with the believer's available reason and evidence and distinguishes rationality from truth. That standard can remain true whether theism is rational or irrational, so it does not itself support or attack any stated bridge.

moveReviews.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moveReviews.attributionBasis: The source span continues Woodford's uninterrupted opening presentation and follows his explicit introduction of the problem of evil.
moveReviews.rationale: The move asserts that mass extinctions, disasters, predation, disease, and other suffering appear gratuitous and conflict with an all-powerful, all-loving God. This directly supports the specific suffering bridge rather than merely the broader central or motion conclusion.

moveReviews.speaker: Simon Edwards
moveReviews.attributionBasis: The source span lies within Edwards's uninterrupted opening case, after the moderator expressly hands the floor to him and he announces three arguments for belief in God.
moveReviews.rationale: The move argues that unguided physical processes leave no rational basis for trusting the mind, while an intelligent creator explains trustworthy minds and an intelligible universe. It exactly supports the rational-mind subsidiary bridge.

moveReviews.speaker: Simon Edwards
moveReviews.attributionBasis: The source span is the explicit conclusion of Edwards's uninterrupted opening case and immediately precedes the moderator's applause request and transition to discussion.
moveReviews.rationale: The move combines the arguments from rationality, teleology, and morality and expressly concludes that God's existence is more probable and belief in God more rational than the alternative. That is direct motion-level support.

moveReviews.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moveReviews.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Woodford about Edwards's argument from reason, Edwards poses a clarification question, and the source span begins with Woodford's direct answer before Edwards responds again.
moveReviews.rationale: The move rejects the inference that evolved minds lack rational warrant, arguing that false representations are costly and natural selection favors broadly accurate beliefs. It directly attacks the unguided-naturalism premise of the rational-mind bridge.

moveReviews.speaker: Simon Edwards
moveReviews.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly asks Edwards to answer Woodford's problem of evil, and the source span occurs during Edwards's continuous response before the floor returns to Woodford.
moveReviews.rationale: The move argues that judgments about suffering must include an eternal afterlife in which God can compensate and restore sufferers. This challenges the inference that apparent suffering is genuinely gratuitous and defeats rational belief.

moveReviews.speaker: Stephen Woodford
moveReviews.attributionBasis: The source span occurs in Woodford's continuous reply to Edwards's treatment of suffering, after the moderator returns the discussion to Woodford and before Edwards asks a further question.
moveReviews.rationale: The move argues that even granting all the positive arguments would establish at most some creator, because suffering remains incompatible with the all-powerful, all-loving God proposed. It directly attacks the central cumulative inference rather than merely restating the pro route.

moveReviews.speaker: Simon Edwards
moveReviews.attributionBasis: After an audience question about whether biblical stories are real, the moderator asks Edwards to answer first; the source span contains that answer, and the moderator subsequently invites Woodford's separate answer.
moveReviews.rationale: The move distinguishes historical, poetic, and parabolic genres in the Bible. That proposition can be true without changing the credibility of any bridge concerning rational theism, evil, salvation confusion, reason, design, or morality.
